# 07. Characters, items and builds

A roguelike character is mostly put together during the run. It starts on a creation screen, but most of what it becomes depends on what the player finds and combines along the way: the wand from the third floor, the mutation offered at level five, the card that turns a mediocre deck into an engine. This chapter covers that whole process. It looks at where character power is stored, how creation, classes and generated stats set up a run, how bodies, traits and identities make characters readable, how upgrade choices are offered and connected into a build space, how much brokenness to allow, and how individual items and the inventory that holds them earn their place.

For a designer this is where replayability comes from. Builds decide whether runs feel different, whether a run is mostly decisions or mostly bookkeeping, and whether players come back to look for the next combination. The speakers include classic roguelike developers, deckbuilder designers, a Magic: The Gathering designer, and people who study traits in The Sims and Crusader Kings. They keep returning to a few levers: where advancement lives, how choices are offered, how densely the pieces connect, how much breakage to tolerate, and whether each trait, item and body part gives the player something legible to act on.

## In brief

- Put power in what the character finds rather than in experience from kills, so the game changes nature as the run goes on and stealth, avoidance and fleeing become real strategies ([Michael Brough 2025, 44:25](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2665); [Michael Brough 2025, 32:21](https://youtu.be/JpX2wWwhKdE?t=1941); [Brian Walker 2016, 7:59](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=479); [Brian Walker 2016, 11:46](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=706); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 15:42](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=942); [John Harris 2016, 5:22](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=322)).
- In a build-heavy game the creation screen is the first pitch, and each creation choice should change how the game plays rather than only how the character looks or what its numbers are ([Ben McGraw 2017, 8:49](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=529); [Ben McGraw 2017, 13:35](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=815); [Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 7:22](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=442)).
- Keep traits few, legible and active: each should do one or two clear things, Wildermyth found that asking players to remember more than two per character dilutes them, and a trait that takes options away from the core loop is a mistake ([Cat Manning 2020, 1:56](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=116); [Brenda Romero 2021, 7:06](https://youtu.be/_vf3HO3wn20?t=426); [Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 4:14](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=254); [Cat Manning 2020, 22:56](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=1376); [Cat Manning 2020, 7:54](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=474)).
- Visible changes to the character's body are among the most memorable kinds of progression, and some games pair them with a cost such as an adaptation penalty, a size limit or a defect taken for extra points ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 8:29](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=509); [Thomas Biskup 2018, 39:46](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=2386); [Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 15:01](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=901)).
- Let chance decide which combinations are on offer and let the player decide how deeply to invest, through a small number of regular, meaningful picks such as choose-one-of-three ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 26:28](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1588); [Andrew Cedotal 2024, 27:08](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1628); [Lisa Brown 2020, 13:40](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=820); [Pandamander 2024, 9:43](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=583)).
- A good upgrade choice changes the style of the run, has no answer that is right regardless of the build, and costs something when you turn it down ([Shawn Main 2021, 13:36](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=816); [Shawn Main 2021, 13:54](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=834); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 22:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1341); [Sersa Victory 2022, 13:07](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=787)).
- Combinations feel like discoveries when they are implicit, built from shared resources, categories and multipliers rather than spelled out in "if X then Y" text ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 5:04](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=304); [Andrew Cedotal 2024, 5:36](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=336); [Ezra Szanton 2025, 18:53](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1133); [Shawn Main 2021, 13:11](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=791); [Courtney Liessen 2024, 3:39](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=219)).
- Keep the build space well connected with only weak clusters and cap how much a single run can collect, because isolated clusters make drafting shallow and builds that can absorb everything blur together ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 11:44](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=704); [Ezra Szanton 2025, 12:54](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=774); [Alice Lai 2021, 13:36](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=816); [Dustin Freeman 2020, 7:55](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=475); [Tim Keenan 2026, 8:36:21](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30981)).
- A rare, earned build that breaks the game is part of a roguelike's promise, so keep strong effects strong and balance them by situation and by what they do rather than by shrinking numbers ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 5:32](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=332); [Courtney Liessen 2024, 2:54](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=174); [Ben McGraw 2017, 21:29](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1289); [Brian Walker 2016, 13:39](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=819); [Dan DiIorio 2025, 8:58](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=538)).
- Make items and inventory pose decisions: give each item a niche and tie its strengths and limits to what the generator varies, and make carrying limits ones the player must commit to before seeing what comes next ([Jasper Cole 2023, 9:55](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=595); [Tom Francis 2023, 7:36](https://youtu.be/3vSCncV5hkI?t=456); [Darren Grey 2020, 21:13](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1273); [Tyriq Plummer 2017, 24:41](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1481); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 17:30](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1050); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 27:17](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1637)).

## Where character power lives: items, experience and the shape of advancement

Before you design a single upgrade, decide where your character's power is stored. It can live in the character (levels, experience points, skills), in what the character carries (weapons, wands, scrolls, rings), or in the world. That one decision sets which builds are viable, whether the player has to fight to keep up, and how much the game changes between the first floor and the last ([Brian Walker 2016, 11:46](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=706); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 15:42](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=942); [Michael Brough 2025, 45:03](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2703)).

### The rogue who becomes a wizard

Michael Brough traces the traditional roguelike answer back to fantasy fiction. In Jack Vance's stories there is a wizard who never casts a spell and whose power is nothing more than a collection of magic items, and Cugel, a thief, declares himself a wizard as soon as he steals some ([Michael Brough 2025, 44:25](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2665)). Brough first read Cugel as a rogue pretending to be a wizard, then realised he does exactly what the real wizard does: being a wizard is defined by owning the items ([Michael Brough 2025, 32:21](https://youtu.be/JpX2wWwhKdE?t=1941)). He sees the same arc in Rogue. You start with a short bow and a sword, thinking about sneaking and positioning, and you end choosing among a large arsenal of magical equipment. Brough stresses that this is not multiclassing: the rules never change, but the decisions you make under them do ([Michael Brough 2025, 44:25](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2665)).

> There being a wizard is defined by having this collection of magic items. — [Michael Brough 2025, 32:21](https://youtu.be/JpX2wWwhKdE?t=1941)

That is the deeper point. Because power arrives as equipment, the progression arc changes the nature of play, not just the numbers: the game you are playing at the end is different from the one you started ([Michael Brough 2025, 45:03](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=2703)).

Brough also gives the lineage. Vancian magic, where discrete memorised spells burn out of the caster's mind when cast, was a storytelling device that became a game mechanic, and it supports the fairy-tale structure in which a hero carries a set of items and solves each challenge with one of them ([Michael Brough 2025, 30:42](https://youtu.be/JpX2wWwhKdE?t=1842)). The rogue's ability to read scrolls at all is an accident of history: the D&D rogue was modelled on Fritz Leiber's Grey Mouser, a thief who had trained as a magician's apprentice, and one character's backstory was generalised to every rogue. Brough notes that a rogue who could not read scrolls is plausible but "not so interesting" ([Michael Brough 2025, 12:14](https://youtu.be/zDKheM-E45I?t=734)).

### Brogue: advancement as items, no experience points

Brogue is the most fully worked example of putting all advancement into equipment, and several talks independently single it out. Brian Walker describes the structure: skills become reusable "skill items" (weapons, armour, staffs, charms, rings), and skill points become single-use scrolls of enchantment, each of which permanently upgrades one item. An enchanted weapon hits harder and more often, armour becomes lighter and more protective, staffs and charms grow stronger and recharge faster. The scrolls look random, but their spawn rate is tightly controlled so every player gets about the same number of points at about the same rate ([Brian Walker 2016, 7:59](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=479)). Brogue's characters start essentially identical, and what changes them is the items and allies found during the run ([Qristy Overton 2021, 3:25](https://youtu.be/zlJNIJOog9M?t=205)).

The second half of Walker's design is removing experience points. With no XP from killing monsters, builds based on avoidance and trickery become viable, and Walker argues they suit roguelikes because deviousness is a skill the player actually has at the keyboard, unlike a warrior's strength, so character skill and player skill line up ([Brian Walker 2016, 11:46](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=706)). Builds that depend on what you happened to find also make wiki lookups much less useful, so the game resists spoilers ([Brian Walker 2016, 11:46](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=706)).

What this buys is improvised classes. Walker names a fire mage, a berserker with an axe and transference, and a stealth assassin, and points out that no line of code defines any of them ([Brian Walker 2016, 10:01](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=601)). Because only a subset of items appears in a given game, players cannot rigidly systematise; vault rooms that offer one item from a set force you to commit before you know what else will appear, and a limited supply of disposable "wild card" items such as teleportation scrolls covers emergencies ([Brian Walker 2016, 10:01](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=601)). Exclusive offers like these vaults come back in the section on shaping the upgrade decision. Eric Billingsley makes the same point from the outside: Brogue has no classes, and choosing which found equipment to invest enchantment into is how you build a class as you go, which is what gives it its run-to-run variety ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 8:16](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=496)). John Harris, in a talk about difficulty, singles out the same choice, removing experience points and tying advancement entirely to equipment, as one he greatly respects ([John Harris 2016, 5:22](https://youtu.be/KY-TmRw5sR8?t=322)).

Billingsley's Into Ruins adopts the model and is candid about the cost. Removing levels and XP loses the feeling of growing stronger by killing monsters. In exchange, with orbs of power as the only progression, the choice of what to power up becomes more meaningful, builds scale differently from each other, and players can flee or use stealth without falling behind ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 15:42](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=942)). Into Ruins also shows how item-based progression lets one object mean different things to different builds: it merges Brogue's staves and wands into staves that never recharge over time but can be refilled by orbs or by wisdom gear on descent. A melee build spends the charges and throws the staff away; a magic build invests orbs or finds the amulet or cloak of wisdom to recharge several staves at once ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 21:22](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1282)).

**In practice:** if you want stealth, avoidance and fleeing to be real strategies, do not pay out power for kills. Put advancement in a controlled-rate resource the player chooses where to spend.

### Skill systems and level-ups: what goes wrong and how games fix it

If power lives in the character, the question becomes how it is earned, and the talks record several failures. Nicholas Feinberg describes Dungeon Crawl's original use-based training, where experience from kills went into whatever skills you used. It sounds intuitive, but straightforward play produced a haphazard mix of skills, and it rewarded "victory dancing": letting a rat hit you for hundreds of turns to train armour, or casting Magic Dart at a wall over and over to train conjurations. Nothing stopped you, and while you could win without doing it, your odds were much worse, so the system was replaced by manual skill allocation ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 4:03](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=243)). The lesson of Crawl's experience is that a training rule the player can farm safely invites farming.

A level-up can also simply be dull. Evan Debenham added a talent system to Shattered Pixel Dungeon, giving points on each level-up to spend on abilities that change decision-making, because many players told him hero levelling was not interesting ([Evan Debenham 2021, 16:36](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=996)). Randomness is another lever: Johnathon Pagnutti describes Fire Emblem: Three Houses rolling each stat's increase separately, with growth rates combining the character and their class, so a level-up can be good (many stats rise) or bad (one or two) ([Johnathon Pagnutti 2026, 2:00](https://youtu.be/DbZe8rWviS0?t=120)). Equipment can level too: John Harris describes Shiren 5 giving swords and shields their own experience, and letting you create new items that appear in dungeons from then on, which subtly changes the whole game; Shiren 6 cut the equipment-experience system, a change Harris considers positive ([John Harris 2024, 25:55](https://youtu.be/0MdNwIHwXy0?t=1555)).

Legibility matters as much as interest. Thomas Biskup says Ultimate ADOM merges ADOM's separate skills, weapon skills and talents into one unified system that looks like skill systems in other games, so people understand it immediately rather than meeting something exotic for its own sake ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 21:49](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1309)).

### The edges: no growth, godhood, and open questions

Some games keep the character fixed. Zeno Rogue's HyperRogue has no hit points, no character growth and no resource management; the character does not grow, but the world advances ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 22:30](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1350)). Josh Ge describes the 7DRL Drakefire Chasm, which goes the other way: it has no items at all, and the young dragon you play progresses only by upgrading its abilities and eating foes to grow larger ([Josh Ge 2018, 9:36](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=576)). David Dunham left deckbuilding out of Thousand Hells for a narrative reason: its characters are iconic heroes who do not change over a story lasting a few weeks, so a changing card set represented nothing, whereas I Was a Teenage Exocolonist, which follows a protagonist growing up over years, suits one ([David Dunham 2026, 7:58](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=478)). Advancement is worth having when it means something in your fiction.

At the other extreme, Zach and Tarn Adams describe Larn and Ragnarok letting high-level characters become god-like, walking through walls or fighting the gods at the end of time, and want Dwarf Fortress to reach that level of world-changing power; as children playing Rogue-like D&D they always died at level two and never got there ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 7:20](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=440)). Darren Grey adds a principle about what the character is relative to everyone else: even though the roguelike player is integrated into the world like a monster (a bomb hurts you as it hurts them), the player should function mechanically differently from other entities, to signal a rogue's separateness from the herd ([Darren Grey 2020, 22:43](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1363)).

Gillian Smith, drawing on progressive pedagogy, offers mechanics nobody has tried: players identifying and self-assessing their own skills during play, inventory that atrophies over time unless it is reinforced, and designers and players talking inside the game rather than in Steam reviews ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:25:26](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5126)). She also suggests asset mapping, in which each learner maps the skills they bring, the team combines the maps, and each person picks areas to grow, could become a roguelike mechanic, while admitting she does not know how ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:23:13](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4993)).

## Character creation and classes: the first build decision

In a build-heavy roguelike the first thing the player does is build. That screen comes before any gameplay, and it is your first chance to show what the game is about.

### Creation as the game's first pitch

Ben McGraw argues that in roguelikes with complex build screens, the build screen fills much of the first minutes and has to sell the game before the gameplay does; Dungeons of Dredmor opens with a choice among 55 skills ([Ben McGraw 2017, 8:49](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=529)). He sets aside appearance customisation and simple stat allocation, which he says say little about how the game will play ([Ben McGraw 2017, 8:49](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=529)). His model is Master of Magic's custom wizard screen, where skills such as Alchemy and Artificer change fundamental rules, and experimenting reveals constraints and hidden options: life and death magic cannot be combined, spreading picks fails while specialising works, and putting all 11 picks into sorcery unlocks uncommon and rare starting spells ([Ben McGraw 2017, 13:35](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=815)).

Jason Grinblat takes the same view for Caves of Qud, citing McGraw's talk and the 1990s 4X games like Master of Magic: character creation is a creative act meant to flood the player's mind with possibilities about what the game is about and what they can do in the world, and he calls it very important and intimate ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 7:22](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=442)). The tradition goes back a long way. Santiago Zapata credits Moria with introducing detailed character creation based on D&D and other RPG systems, plus spellbooks, which made creation a fundamental part of roguelikes; you can spend a long time tweaking a character into what you want ([Santiago Zapata 2022, 15:42](https://youtu.be/y6WCq0jYbHo?t=942)).

> It's supposed to just sort of like flood your brain with possibilities. — [Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 7:22](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=442)

### Structures that multiply starting variety

A creation screen needs many distinct starts without a balance problem that grows with every option. Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup's (DCSS) answer, as bhauth describes it, is to split creation into species (permanent effects) and background (starting equipment and skills): a Minotaur Fighter is one species and one background, and dividing things this way multiplies combinations while keeping balance manageable ([bhauth 2020, 1:33](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=93)).

Caves of Qud makes its first choice a fork between two different build systems. True Kin, pure-strain descendants of the arcology dwellers, cannot mutate but can install cybernetic implants; mutants get the broad mutation list ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 3:07](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=187)). Its castes and callings (Marauder, Apostle, Tinker, Water Merchant) work like classes, but mostly just set starting skills and adjust stats, because the mutations matter much more ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 18:52](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=1132)). Phillip Daigle's Rogue's Gate adds a third axis: alongside race and class you choose a starting party, which determines your starting companions, equipment and a slight narrative nudge, so each run opens with a different flavour ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 4:04](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=244)). Thomas Biskup's Ultimate ADOM shows the data side: a race entity defines body structure and the nine attributes as dice expressions rolled per instance, so an orc's strength of 2d3+7 gives 9 to 13 ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 21:57](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=1317)).

### Classes: worth the content?

The talks do not agree on whether classes earn their cost. Brian Walker argues that adding classes is a poor way to maximise hours of fun per unit of content: unless they are perfectly balanced one class is strongest and each class has a dominant build, and optimal players look it up. He did exactly that with the Diablo II sorceress and found the rest of the content wasted for him. He grants that classes suit games inheriting an audience that wants diverse play styles ([Brian Walker 2016, 7:19](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=439)).

David Brevik's account of Diablo cuts the other way. Diablo's design was that anyone could do anything, just better or worse, with classes differing mainly in casting and attack speeds; balanced in theory, it produced a soup where average players did not know which direction to go ([David Brevik 2023, 22:57](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=1377)). Diablo II responded by guiding and restricting players: distinct paths within a class (Amazon bows versus spears), off-class options still possible but harder through stat requirements, and item sets, crafting and skill synergies as late-game combination play ([David Brevik 2023, 23:36](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=1416)). So Walker's problem is a dominant build inside each class, and Brevik's is too much freedom without firm classes. Which one bites depends on your audience: Walker's optimiser looks up the dominant build, Brevik's average player is lost without one.

Andrea Roberts adds that choosing a class is also choosing how complex your game will be. Roundguard's warrior, rogue and wizard target increasing complexity, and players who picked the front-and-centre warrior concluded the game was not complicated enough. A complexity meter on the selection screen fixed it by making clear this was a choice they were making ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 19:46](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1186)). Class rules that cut against ordinary play can also catch players out: John Harris describes Advanced Rogue 7's paladins and rangers, who follow a code of conduct under which attacking a sleeping monster can strip their special powers, which trips up players used to ordinary roguelike play ([John Harris 2021, 21:48](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=1308)).

### Generated stats and rerolling

Random starting numbers create an incentive to reroll. Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner keep Wildermyth's random starting stat bonuses small, because if they are too impactful players reroll heroes until they get the stats they want, which isn't fun; stats earned during the adventure should matter more ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 4:48](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=288)). Jim Shepard's Dungeonmans removes the option outright: players name a hero before rolling stats, and dismissing the result stores the name, so that person may reappear as a shopkeeper or bandit. It drew angry mail and a negative Steam review, which Shepard accepts because the game is not for that player ([Jim Shepard 2016, 10:58](https://youtu.be/_Si626-Y_q0?t=658)).

Small generated differences still matter when death is permanent. Stella Vermilion explains that each Pokémon gets hidden per-stat values from 0 to 31 and a nature that raises one stat by 10% and lowers another by 10%; in a Nuzlocke (a self-imposed permadeath run) whether an Incineroar knocks out an Aegislash before dying can depend on whether it rolled maximum or minimum stats ([Stella Vermilion 2026, 8:51:28](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31888)). Keep generated stats small, but do not assume small means irrelevant.

The converse is a stat that does nothing. Erik Osheim and Robert Au describe Angband removing charisma and store haggling, a break with D&D tradition, because charisma had no meaningful gameplay impact beyond occasionally being drained ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 16:39](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=999)). Jeff Olson regrets Alphaman's Intelligence stat for the same reason, and says the line it took in the character box would have been better spent on something interesting, like a third mutation ([Jeff Olson 2023, 6:18](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=378)).

## Bodies as builds: mutation, grafting and transformation

A build can also be written on the character's body. Instead of a number going up, the character gains a tail, a dragon's head or a robot arm torn from an enemy, and the change is both a power and something the player can see.

### Grafting, and why visible change sticks

Thomas Biskup's Ultimate ADOM grafting lets players collect body parts from other beings and attach them to themselves or others for new powers: a dragon head to breathe fire, spider spinnerets that add a "spin a web" option, a ghoul's hand for a paralytic touch ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 14:46](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=886)). Biskup says body structure becomes interesting once you can do something with it, hacking off parts and then grafting them, and frames grafting as the living-being counterpart to an item crafting system, both made easy by components ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 14:46](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=886); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 25:02](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1502)). Crucially, it has costs. The engine knows your normal body plan, and deviating from it temporarily lowers attributes such as dexterity until you adapt (four untrained legs are hard to control), while size limits forbid some combinations outright: a gnome cannot take an ancient red wyrm's head because it would be squashed. Biskup's summary is that everything has a price ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 39:46](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=2386)).

Wildermyth shows why visible change is worth building. Belanger and Wagner say visible transformations such as a wolf head are among their most successful forms of hero progression, because they change combat abilities and story events can reference them reliably ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 8:29](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=509)).

> The player might forget something their hero did in the past but definitely won't forget their hero has a wolf head — [Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 8:29](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=509)

Julian Day, writing poetry around roguelikes, notes how common transformation is in the genre, a kitten growing into a cat, ADOM mutations, NetHack polypiling, and argues it matters because it promotes the belief that things can change in an understandable way ([Julian Day 2020, 14:29](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=869)).

### The mutation lineage

Mutation as a build system appears in many games, and the shared features are worth noticing. Caves of Qud is the broadest. Mutants assemble a build from over seventy mutations, from animal parts such as tails, stingers and extra legs to mental powers such as teleporting or making time clones ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 7:46](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=466)). The list is wide enough that the developers invite audiences to name any archetype and build it: a "spider person" comes together from multiple legs, spinnerets, night vision and corrosive gas ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 4:08](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=248)). On levelling up, mutation points either raise an existing mutation (more pyrokinesis damage and heat; more speed from multiple legs rather than more legs) or buy a new one for four points, chosen from three random offers such as time dilation, cryokinesis and force bubble ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 23:19](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=1399)). And Qud makes drawbacks a resource: you can take one defect, such as a beak, blinking tic (random teleporting), spontaneous combustion or an evil twin, in exchange for extra mutation points ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 15:01](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=901); [Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 7:13](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=433)).

Other games hand the player less control. In DCSS, Demonspawn gain powerful mutations in three stages as they level, horns that eventually grant an extra melee attack but forbid helmets, for example; you may start with magic-user intentions, receive stealth and melee mutations, and have to change direction ([Tariq et al. 2016, 22:53](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=1373)). Jeff Olson's Alphaman gave characters random physical and mental mutations, 17 and 13 of them, mostly adapted from Gamma World, that worked something like classes: some activated (sonic attack, life leech), some always on (a tough exoskeleton), quills fired periodically as a ranged weapon ([Jeff Olson 2023, 7:19](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=439)). NetHack's version is eating: certain corpses grant intrinsic resistances and abilities, dragons for elemental resistances and a floating eye for telepathy, which Adeon uses while blind to scout levels ([Adeon 2017, 32:30](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=1950)). Alexander Birke's Sea of Rifts extends mutation to the crew: a paper-doll portrait system lets crew members visibly change as they are exposed to the world's strange energies ([Alexander Birke 2024, 22:25](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=1345)).

The design choice running through these is how much say the player has over which change arrives, from Qud's pick-one-of-three to Demonspawn's forced adaptation to NetHack's choose-what-you-eat.

### Bodies made of parts

Cogmind makes the body a loadout. Josh Ge's founding idea, taken from a single forum post, was to take the parts of your enemies and make them part of you, growing bigger and more powerful; destroyed robots explode into parts you can pick up ([Josh Ge 2016, 8:57](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=537)). His 7DRL version proved the core mechanic was fun before it became a full-time project, and it already had rampant item destruction that forced frequent rebuilding ([Josh Ge 2018, 10:05](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=605)). That destruction is what keeps a parts-based body from settling into one final build.

Ge's Polybot-7 is a controlled experiment on player control. It changes one rule: nearby parts automatically fly over and attach, and can only be removed by being destroyed. Taking away the choice over attachment made the game play extremely differently, and in Ge's words, the entire game feeling changed ([Josh Ge 2018, 11:00](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=660)).

Other games swap the whole body or build around one ability. Ultimate ADOM's pentagram of possession swaps souls between two beings that step on it, so you can inhabit a goblin, a dragon or a wall that cannot open doors for lack of hands; Biskup's motivation is to explore the game more deeply than playing dwarves, elves and humans ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 26:15](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=1575)). Jonathan Lessard's Chogue keeps chess's pawn promotion but promotes pawns to queens when they reach a wall, since a generated Rogue map has no reliable far edge; players can promote almost immediately, which is fine because queens move much faster in that world ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 15:28](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=928)). Benet Devereux built a small roguelike around the tardigrade's most famous ability, going dormant to survive extremes, so the goal became surviving a set time and the rest of the design was generating extreme situations ([Benet Devereux 2022, 2:47](https://youtu.be/0iNW5AYYWWw?t=167)).

### Selection without control: Test Tube Titans

Gabriel Koenig's Test Tube Titans takes mutation furthest. The generator produces endless creature configurations, and the player's job is to select which to keep, so procedural generation itself becomes the core mechanic and the player makes the discoveries ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 9:16](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=556)). Each mutation step offers three choices from the same process, and a radiation dial sets the size of the leap: high radiation makes bigger jumps that often take the wrong turn, low radiation is safer but takes more cycles ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 9:56](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=596)). Koenig started mostly random to avoid too many options, then let players unlock finer control later, such as crossbreeding and selective mutation of only the legs, which reduces chaos by letting players choose where change happens without controlling the outcome; which manual upgrades each titan can take is randomised, and multiplayer simplifies everything to accept or reroll ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 13:59](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=839)).

The result is ownership without control. A creature built from many compounding selections is one of a kind, and players quickly identified with their titans even though they never directly controlled outcomes ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 11:21](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=681)). With no designer-intended way to play each titan, players balance build, stats and aesthetics with no correct choice, developing a specialised mastery they can invest in or abandon ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 12:34](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=754)).

**In practice:** pair every body change with a cost or constraint (adaptation penalties, size limits, defects, lost equipment slots), keep the change visible, and decide deliberately where the player sits between choosing each change and only reacting to it.

## Traits, personality and identity: characters players can read

When a game generates characters, their traits are how the player reads them. A trait is a promise that this character is someone in particular, and the talks agree that the promise has to be both understandable and mechanically real.

### What a trait is for

Cat Manning defines a trait as a simple in-game word, often binary and deliberately oversimplified, that gestures at a generated character's personality and offers clear hooks into the game's mechanics, so players can imagine and extrapolate stories. Traits help players parse dense systems that would otherwise be overwhelming data ([Cat Manning 2020, 1:56](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=116)). Brenda Romero adds a rule from Empire of Sin: the player must never be stuck with a bad trait. There should always be a way around it, or nobody will choose that character, and characters need to evolve with play or every game is the same ([Brenda Romero 2021, 8:39](https://youtu.be/_vf3HO3wn20?t=519)).

> I wanted to make sure that the player never felt stuck with a bad trait there should always be a way around the situation — [Brenda Romero 2021, 8:39](https://youtu.be/_vf3HO3wn20?t=519)

### Trait sprawl

Three independent sources warn about too many traits, or traits that do too much. Manning's analysis of The Sims 3 finds many traits that are perceptually distinct in name but mechanically overlapping: Flirty unlocks romantic actions at a lower score while Irresistible builds score faster, an effect players cannot really tell apart, and Friendly, Charismatic and Schmoozer blur the same way. She ties this to Kate Compton's "10,000 bowls of oatmeal" problem, in which what matters is perceptual uniqueness rather than mathematical uniqueness; here the differences live only in how players interpret the words ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:11:26](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=4286)). Expansion packs made it worse, since new traits could only draw on base-game systems and so felt like variants of existing traits or shallow showcases for a new feature ([Cat Manning 2020, 6:31](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=391)). A few ornate flavour traits are fine, Manning says, but too many make players doubt whether any trait matters mechanically; a trait need not be beautiful on its own but must fit its context, and how much to surface depends on how much of your loop is discovery versus acting on known information ([Cat Manning 2020, 21:08](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=1268)).

Romero reached a similar limit from the other side: each Empire of Sin trait triggers only one or two effects, because traits that did more became a spider web players could not understand, even though traits collectively touch much of the game ([Brenda Romero 2021, 7:06](https://youtu.be/_vf3HO3wn20?t=426)). Belanger and Wagner put a number on attention: Wildermyth has 11 personality traits, but only a hero's primary and secondary traits matter most, because asking players to remember more than two per hero dilutes them ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 4:14](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=254)).

Even a realistic, interesting trait can fail if it fights the core loop. The Sims 3's Absent-Minded trait randomly dropped queued actions, so players had to monitor those Sims constantly; Manning calls it a trait that tied story to system but took options away instead of opening them ([Cat Manning 2020, 7:54](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=474)). She also warns smaller games not to copy The Sims 3's expressive, loosely mechanical traits: they worked there because the game already had appearance, decor and career systems for players to express personality through, and most developers should weave traits into their core systems from the start ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:15:34](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=4534)).

### Making traits active

Manning's fix is to make traits do something rather than forbid something. Crediting Tanya Short, she contrasts Crusader Kings II's chaste trait as a list of what you cannot do, which is boring, with a chaste character who runs around haranguing everyone having sex, which creates surprising play ([Cat Manning 2020, 22:56](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=1376)). Crusader Kings III's stress system shows the same principle working: rulers acting against their character accumulate stress toward breakdown, so a compassionate pagan ruler struggles to gain piety and traits become part of the player's decisions rather than passive bonuses ([Cat Manning 2020, 19:56](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=1196)).

Tom Francis's Heat Signature shows traits that reshape a whole run. Glitch-sick means teleporting knocks you out, so you teleport into empty rooms to recover; Technophobe means nothing recharges, making self-charging gear worthless; Shaky makes guns inaccurate and pushes you to gadgets, with an inverse trait pushing toward guns ([Tom Francis 2023, 14:11](https://youtu.be/3vSCncV5hkI?t=851)). Each one filters the run through a constraint, which is the active trait in its purest form. (Francis applies the same thinking to tools; see *Item design* below.)

Structure helps keep traits legible. Manning notes The Sims 3 replaced The Sims 2's five-axis point system with orthogonal traits (Friendly does not imply Party Animal) that the game does not correlate, apart from a few binary pairs such as Slob and Neat, leaving players to connect them ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:10:38](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=4238)). Asked which three dimensions she would pick, Manning chose beliefs and values, how a character relates to others, and how likely they are to act on their beliefs given society's defaults ([Cat Manning 2020, 24:02](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=1442)). Romero divides Empire of Sin's traits into categories with different rates of change: fixed historical traits (immigrant, fell on hard times), life-lesson traits absent in very young gangsters, physical traits such as the player favourite Hair Trigger, and the most malleable personality traits earned in play ([Brenda Romero 2021, 7:16](https://youtu.be/_vf3HO3wn20?t=436)). Malleability is tied to age, so an older gangster near the end of his career arrives settled, while younger ones can be shaped more by the player ([Brenda Romero 2021, 9:19](https://youtu.be/_vf3HO3wn20?t=559)). And when a character leaves player control, hospitalised or away on a mission, Romero treats it as licence to give them new traits on return, such as a fear of plants, because the player never saw what happened ([Brenda Romero 2021, 14:31](https://youtu.be/_vf3HO3wn20?t=871)).

Characterisation also comes from relationships and possessions. Wildermyth's friendships, romances, rivalries and family ties form randomly or by choice and carry both story impact and combat buffs (romance makes a hero hit harder against whoever attacks their lover), and players become very invested in them ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 5:16](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=316)). Wildermyth also forbids swapping weapons between heroes: when swapping was allowed, gear felt separate from heroes, and now gear characterises its owner, appears in combat and comics, and reminds the player of the event that granted it ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 6:58](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=418)).

### Identity: what your traits say about people

Traits and stats carry beliefs whether you intend them or not. Florence Smith Nicholls points out that archetypes, reality TV's girl next door and vixen or roguelike classes inherited from tabletop RPGs, are often gendered and can become toxic, and asks designers to examine how they use them ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 3:32](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=212)). Xalavier Nelson Jr. gives a concrete case: in Oblivion, Redguards are combat-strong and pain-resistant while lighter-skinned Imperials get social traits, so a Black player who wants a talking-and-lockpicking style must choose a character who does not look like him. His wider point is that any differentiation makes the differences meaningful and invites players to read patterns into them ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 23:30](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1410)).

There are alternatives to a menu. Aaron Reed's Hollywood Visionary builds a character's public persona from many expressive choices instead of a list of gender options: choosing a signature fashion item and then wearing something else to a party, choosing what friends and business associates call you, accepting or rejecting labels, choosing love interests ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 9:17](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=557)). Alexandra Leonhart notes that roguelike role-play already lets players define characters against their stats, a strong character played as a pacifist vegetarian magic enthusiast, or a NetHack pacifist run, and connects this to Preciado's and Stryker's ideas of bodily self-definition ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:22:43](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30163)). Her cyberpunk prototype inverts cyber-psychosis: instead of losing humanity as they merge with technology, characters level up through decisions and introspection about their identity ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:26:56](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30416)). Nathan Savant offers a frame for that kind of design: a progression tree represents the kind of person a character can imagine becoming, so mentors can unlock trees, trauma can remove them, and quests or items can grant temporary skills ([Nathan Savant 2021, 9:51](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=591)).

**In practice:** use few traits, make each one legible and active, wire them into your core loop rather than bolting them on, and look hard at what your trait and stat assignments imply about the kinds of people they describe.

## Shaping the upgrade decision: offers, drafts and sets

The sections so far have been about what a character is made of. The rest of the chapter is about how those pieces reach the player and fit together, starting with the moment of choosing one. The content of an upgrade system is only half of it. The other half is the shape of the decision: how many options appear, how often, how big each pick is, and what the player gives up by taking one ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 27:08](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1628); [Lisa Brown 2020, 13:40](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=820); [Alexander King 2025, 10:26](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=626); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 22:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1341)).

### Drafting in the front, constructed in the back

Andrew Cedotal frames the problem as a Goldilocks one. A purely constructed upgrade system, where the player knows everything and can pick anything, is always there and always the same. A purely random one takes away decision responsibility, like playing a card game with truly random blind decks, something he says every team tries once ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 26:28](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1588)). His answer is what he calls the "drafting mullet": chance limits which combos are on offer, because you can only pursue a combo if a component turns up early enough to draw the rest, but once a combo is open the player controls how deeply to invest in it. The familiar choose-one-of-three upgrade offer does this neatly ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 27:08](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1628)).

> It is drafting in the front, constructed in the back. — [Andrew Cedotal 2024, 27:08](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1628)

Cedotal borrows Soren Johnson's distinction between luck that comes before a decision and luck that comes after it ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 27:08](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1628)). The offer is the pre-decision luck; what the player does with it is theirs.

### A few deliberate decisions, regularly spaced

How many of these decisions should there be? Lisa Brown, writing from the point of view of a player with low strategy motivation, prefers roguelikes that hand her a small number of meaningful, reactive decisions at regular points: Nuclear Throne's mutation pick, Slay the Spire's post-combat card choice, arranging cards after each drop in Loot Rascals. That gives a sense of strategy without heavy cognitive load; FTL lost her because its load was higher ([Lisa Brown 2020, 13:40](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=820)). Pandamander makes a compatible point in psychological terms: the slow, deliberate "System 2" choice of picking an upgrade balances the fast, reflexive "System 1" play of combat, and satisfying roguelikes need both. They cite Anthony Giovannetti saying Slay the Spire is about card picking, and in their own game the chosen dog breed shapes which runs and challenges the player pursues ([Pandamander 2024, 9:43](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=583)).

The same audience shows where the limit sits. Brown bounced off Rogue Legacy because of its between-run skill tree. She grants it is only about four layers deep, but beyond about four choices is too much for her; she builds to reach a goal, not to express herself ([Lisa Brown 2020, 24:50](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1490)). A large tree can serve players who enjoy composing a character, but it costs you the players who want a quick, practical pick with immediate impact.

### What makes a single choice good

Shawn Main gives two tests. First, the choice should be impactful enough to change the style of the run; he points to Hades, where getting a particular Daedalus Hammer upgrade or not gives a meaningfully different experience ([Shawn Main 2021, 13:36](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=816)). Second, good choices recontextualise each other: no option is definitively best, because its value depends on what you have already built, and it in turn shapes later choices. In his Lab of Legends, a choice between a power that boosts units that survive damage and one that boosts big units has no right answer apart from the deck you have ([Shawn Main 2021, 13:54](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=834)).

The other lever is cost. Cole Wehrle deliberately made the decisions in Oath, even large sandbox ones, near-binary: either this or that, so the player knows the path not taken could haunt them. At game end the player holding the people's favour makes three piles of three cards and keeps one, banishing the rest to a dispossessed pile, possibly for ten to twenty generations; players are dealt two legacies and keep one. The resulting regret is what makes the game's history feel consequential ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 22:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1341)).

Sersa Victory catalogues ways roguelikes build this kind of exclusive choice. In Brogue's treasure rooms, the vaults Walker describes above, lifting an item off its pedestal drops cages on the rest, so the player chooses from play style, build, run history and predictions; Forays into Norrendrin's skill shrines come in pairs and accepting one makes the other inert ([Sersa Victory 2022, 13:07](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=787)). In her own Rogue remake, praying at an early altar makes the player a lesser priestess but forfeits becoming a high priestess deeper down, so the player weighs how badly she needs help now against her confidence in reaching the stronger role ([Sersa Victory 2022, 17:36](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1056)). Her list of other choice-rich mechanics is a useful palette: trading strength for armour class, a token whose cash-in value grows the longer you wait, a power that grows with the number of adjacent monsters, cursed items stronger than normal but risky on each use, choosing a trap's punishment, and an extra life with a significant cost ([Sersa Victory 2022, 24:13](https://youtu.be/TeURjrAYFEU?t=1453)).

Choices can also be nudged by the map rather than the menu. In Rift Wizard, circles of power discount spells of one school by a skill point while the player stands on them, so where you are affects what you buy; Dylan White weighs which level to enter by its circle and by shrines that upgrade particular schools ([Dylan White 2020, 8:03](https://youtu.be/VVRomN99Ygw?t=483)).

### Granularity: one card or a set at a time

Alexander King argues that the size of each pick is a design choice in its own right. Singleton drafting, adding cards one by one, is high-friction: it needs many decisions, which pushes deckbuilding out across the whole run, and because every card must be evaluated individually in a deck that keeps changing, there is an upper limit on how complex any single card can be ([Alexander King 2025, 4:47](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=287)). His alternative is set-based deckbuilding, starting from the observation that a game has a fixed complexity budget and the question is how you spend it: sets spend it on fewer but more agonising decisions, comparing six cards against six others rather than one against one, which King considers a good thing ([Alexander King 2025, 10:26](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=626)).

Card Hunter is his main example. Each hero has a 36-card deck; three heroes would mean 108 cards to manage one at a time. Instead each equipped item contributes a group of cards (three, or six for weapons), so a full deck takes about ten picks instead of 36, and the interface shows what an item gives, what it replaces and the resulting deck ([Alexander King 2025, 8:25](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=505)). Tabletop set-based games work the same way, assembling a 40-card deck from four themed sets of ten ([Alexander King 2025, 9:59](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=599)). King lists what sets buy you:

- **Cards that need not stand alone.** Sets allow thematic bundles and pre-built mini-combos. A huge pickaxe in Card Hunter gives an armour-ignoring impale card, strong cards with drawbacks and an "unwieldy" drawback card; Card Quest's cursed dagger gives item-unique cards that build up a resource that eventually hurts you ([Alexander King 2025, 10:54](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=654)).
- **Control over composition.** Because typically only the boots slot gives movement cards, Card Hunter players end up with roughly the right number of them, so more archetypes are viable and pruning and filtering mechanics are needed less ([Alexander King 2025, 12:23](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=743)).
- **A shift from building to playing.** Singleton building is assembling an engine from parts; set building is finding working parts and building a car that is fun to drive. King suggests this suits roguelike deckbuilders where deckbuilding is not the main focus, and notes Deep Sky Derelicts and Trials of Fire still assemble sets over a run ([Alexander King 2025, 14:21](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=861)).

Treating cards as inventory goes back further. Dream Quest replaces the inventory with a deck: gaining equipment means adding cards, and Dan Recht observes that this means you can only improve your odds in a fight, never control the outcome directly ([Dan Recht 2017, 5:39](https://youtu.be/FnJxkId-1eE?t=339)). Chris McCormick's Smallest Quest, a minimal roguelike for children, collects items as cards in the same spirit, inspired by Patience Rogue ([Chris McCormick 2021, 6:00](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=360)).

**In practice:** decide the size of each decision (one item, a set, a class) and its frequency together, against the complexity budget you can afford. Make each offer small enough to read quickly, impactful enough to change the run, and exclusive enough that the road not taken costs something ([Alexander King 2025, 10:26](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=626); [Shawn Main 2021, 13:36](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=816); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 22:21](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=1341)).

## Synergy and comboness: why combinations feel like discoveries

Players of build-heavy roguelikes are chasing combinations. Several talks try to say precisely what that thing is, because the definition tells you how to build it.

### What a combo is

Ezra Szanton starts from drafting. If every card has a fixed value, card A is simply better than card B and drafting is trivial. Value has to change with the game state for drafting to be interesting; it could depend on the environment or the upcoming enemies, but a deckbuilder already has a deck, so making a card's value depend on the other cards is the natural lever. That is synergy: two cards worth more than the sum of their parts ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 5:46](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=346)).

Andrew Cedotal tightens the definition. "Worth more than its parts" has a loophole: if A alone is worth 10 and B plus C together beat their parts but still fall short of A plus something, nobody picks B and C, and nobody calls it a combo. So a combo is a subset of upgrades whose value, counting conditional effects, exceeds the highest unconditional value of any subset of the same size ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 3:51](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=231)). He adds a second dimension: comboness is a matter of degree, depending both on how far the conditional value exceeds the best unconditional pick and on how non-obvious that value is ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 5:36](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=336)). Common usage excludes explicit conditional text ("C is worth 3 if B is present"), but rewrite the same maths through tokens (B grants a foo token, C gains value per foo token) and players call it a combo. The less obvious a combination, the more comboness players attribute to it ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 5:04](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=304)).

The payoff is a feeling. James Cartlidge describes one of the best moments in a roguelite like Vampire Survivors as hitting on a powerful synergy, wondering whether it will work, and then watching it destroy everything, so that the player feels they have broken the game ([James Cartlidge et al. 2024, 19:37](https://youtu.be/ujKlmvfpNMo?t=1177)). Pandamander describes the slower version in Slay the Spire's Grand Finale, a card that only works with an empty draw pile and lots of draw. It usually looks useless, but once a run starts collecting cards like Acrobatics, the player begins anticipating the combo; once in a blue moon it lines up, the kind of moment people make videos about ([Pandamander 2024, 3:26](https://youtu.be/KtQh4QrsUzs?t=206)). Both the thrill of the gamble and the long anticipation depend on the player suspecting a combination before they have confirmed it.

### How combos are built and signalled

Alice Lai contrasts two ways games let players find combinations. In The Binding of Isaac, Swallowed Penny (coins when damaged), Bloody Penny (health on coin pickup) and Money = Power (damage scales with coins) are each mediocre, but together with a blood donation machine they become an engine of near-infinite coins, health and damage, and players can intuit the synergy from the effects themselves ([Alice Lai 2021, 3:39](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=219)). Enter the Gungeon instead scripts its combos on the back end; the only hint is shared theming, so players learn that bee-related items will produce bee combos ([Alice Lai 2021, 4:29](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=269)). Isaac's approach yields combos with high comboness in Cedotal's sense; Gungeon's trades discovery-through-reasoning for a learnable signal.

Hades, Lai's own game, builds combos by aiming several upgrades at the same ability. An upgrade either removes a base ability's downside or amplifies its upside: Ares' Blade Rift cast hits hard but is slow and easy to walk out of, so Engulfing Vortex pulls enemies in and Vicious Cycle adds damage the longer they stay ([Alice Lai 2021, 8:04](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=484)). The gun's secondary attack stacks Cluster Bomb, Rocket Bomb and Dionysus' Flourish into a rocket shotgun that applies damage over time far faster than the player normally could ([Alice Lai 2021, 6:59](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=419)).

Szanton orders the sources of synergy from obvious to obscure, which doubles as a menu for designers ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 18:53](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1133)):

1. Explicit callouts.
2. Resource generation and use (cards that make fire tokens and cards that spend them).
3. Chains of events (heal, then draw on heal; these can loop).
4. Multiplicative relationships (Balatro's chips times mult; poison that decays is multiplicative with itself).
5. Benefiting from the same gameplay choice (in Mr. Magpie, perks that reward flipping in a checkerboard pattern synergise with each other).

Courtney Liessen adds a powerful case of the multiplicative kind: let upgrades change the conversion equation itself. With 10 strength, +1 strength gives +1 damage, but +1 to the strength-to-damage multiplier gives +10, and once players see that, they start wondering whether every multiplier could be raised. The indirection makes items feel worth far more than their face value ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 3:39](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=219)).

Underneath all of this is shared material. Shawn Main argues good choices are modular: they act on the same building blocks, so systems readily interact. Dicey Dungeons' items all manipulate dice in finite, discrete ways. A choice between a longsword and ballroom dancing gives nothing to interact unless, as in Boyfriend Dungeon, both affect the same outcomes; cosmetic and gameplay choices running in parallel never meet ([Shawn Main 2021, 13:11](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=791)). Correlation can do similar work for gear. Alex Byaly notes that in Tales of Maj'Eyal, if mental save and confusion immunity tend to appear together, a player chasing full confusion immunity can afford to neglect mental save, so correlated stats let players plan ([Alex Byaly 2022, 8:57](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=537)).

### Case: Rift Wizard and Noita

Rift Wizard shows a whole game built on these principles. Players buy any spell in any order with skill points, and the many synergies and dependencies between spells and passive skills make building feel like a trading card game ([Dylan White 2020, 3:35](https://youtu.be/VVRomN99Ygw?t=215)). Flame Gate spawns a short-lived fire elemental each time you cast a fire spell, as long as you neither move nor cast anything else, so it rewards a stationary fire build and makes every step a cost ([Dylan White 2020, 6:27](https://youtu.be/VVRomN99Ygw?t=387)). Ghost Fire summons a fire ghost when an enemy takes dark and fire damage in the same turn; a dark sorcery cannot be cast in the same turn as Fireball, so Dylan White pairs it with the Nightmare aura, which randomly deals dark or arcane damage nearby. Once running, the ghosts' own fire attacks spawn more ghosts and the level fills up, out of control in the player's favour ([Dylan White 2020, 18:21](https://youtu.be/VVRomN99Ygw?t=1101)). Noita makes combination its core: Arvi Teikari counts the wand system, where spells placed in a wand's slots combine into new effects, as one of the game's three pillars alongside its roguelite structure and pixel physics ([Arvi Teikari 2021, 5:34](https://youtu.be/huMHQGr8PgM?t=334)).

**In practice:** build synergy through shared resources, categories and multipliers rather than explicit "if X then Y" text, because implicit links read as discoveries. Give players enough to suspect a combination (intuitable effects, shared theming, a card that looks like it wants something) before the run confirms it ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 5:04](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=304); [Ezra Szanton 2025, 14:54](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=894); [Alice Lai 2021, 4:29](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=269)).

## Designing the build space: networks, silos and run-to-run variety

Individual combos are local. The build space is the whole set of upgrades and how they connect, and it decides whether drafting stays interesting on the hundredth run.

### The synergy network

Ezra Szanton's model treats cards as nodes and pairwise synergies as edges. That explicit network approximates the mental model experienced players build up and use when drafting. Adding an edge changes which card is correct: a lonely, weak card C becomes the right pick when you already hold several Bs once a B-C edge exists. Szanton later measures edges as the increase in win percentage from holding both cards, keeping only meaningfully positive ones ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 9:13](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=553)). His goal is improvisation and depth: he was delighted when Mr. Magpie's best player told a newcomer that you can't shoot for one thing every time and have to roll with the punches ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 4:52](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=292)).

He names two failure states and a target:

- **Sparse.** Networks start sparse early in development, but sparseness can creep in late too. If the challenge scales faster than most synergies, say a higher-order polynomial against linear synergies, players ignore the linear ones and chase only the few that keep pace with the power curve ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 10:46](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=646)).
- **Siloed.** Clusters with few connections between them make drafting shallow. In Hellscaper, Szanton designed all-fire and all-monster sets that were fun to play but not to draft: players spotted the five builds, took one good card and put their blinders on. Silos also let players arrive with a pre-planned strategy, which undercuts improvisation ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 11:44](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=704)).
- **Healthy.** Well connected, with weak clusters: build-arounds still exist, but pivot points let players branch out or switch strategies mid-run ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 12:54](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=774)).

Two tools shape the network. Because card text must stay short, overlapping categories are the succinct way to create many edges and join clusters. Balatro's Smiley Face joker refers to face cards, which touches the network more broadly than its text suggests; Szanton suggests overlapping slices (vowels and consonants plus a "piano notes" set) and effect categories like "do X" versus "when X happens" ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 14:54](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=894)). Anti-synergies prune the network and add depth: compounding downsides, competition for the same resource, diminishing returns, conflicting gameplay choices, such as too many self-damage cards, too many expensive cards or defence beyond what enemies deal. He advises keeping them implicit, because players find discovering anti-synergies less exciting than synergies, and explicit callouts exist mainly to excite new players ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 21:49](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1309)).

### The opposite instinct: bounded silos

Alice Lai describes Hades taking what looks like the opposite approach, for legibility. Each upgrade system has a clearly bounded job: Hermes and the Mirror make you plainly better, hammers and aspects change weapon attacks, gods add status effects and casts. Seeing a hammer on a reward door tells the player they will be offered an attack modification, so they can plan without holding the whole possibility space in their head ([Alice Lai 2021, 11:50](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=710)). To keep that true, an idea that crosses silos is split: no god boon may both change your secondary attack and add a debuff; instead it becomes a standalone debuff boon and a separate secondary-attack change ([Alice Lai 2021, 23:37](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1417)).

The positions are less opposed than they look. Szanton's warning is about clusters of cards that only work with each other; Lai's silos are about what kind of change each reward source can make, and her combos still cut across them (the rocket shotgun mixes hammers with a Dionysus boon). Both want the player to improvise. Lai says the combos that worked for the team were intentional, player-driven and not available every run; keepsakes give experienced players some control over which gods appear, but a desired combination could not simply be chased down every time ([Alice Lai 2021, 14:33](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=873)). Where they differ is in what they are protecting: Szanton the depth of each draft, Lai the player's ability to understand an offer at a glance.

### How much a run can hold

Lai's numbers show the arithmetic of variety. Players see about two hammers per run and picking one blocks others, so Hades offers about nine hammer options per weapon, a figure found through playtests and credited to design lead Amir. After one choice, around six remain at the most conservative estimate, enough that consecutive runs with the same weapon don't show the same options ([Alice Lai 2021, 12:31](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=751)). Too many upgrades per run has the opposite effect: with three or four hammers, gun runs always ended as a triple-quintuple rocket launcher and sword runs as a massive area-of-effect parry. A bug that let players game the reward table for four hammers produced exactly this "powerful sludge", which Lai links to Kate Compton's 10,000 bowls of oatmeal, the same problem Manning found in Sims traits ([Alice Lai 2021, 13:36](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=816)). Capping what a single run can collect is what keeps runs distinct.

Dustin Freeman makes the same point at the scale of a whole fiction: "kitchen sink" universes where any power is attainable with enough effort are boring, because choices reduce to quantity of effort; he cites Dragon Ball Z, where Goku can probably do anything if he trains enough ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 7:55](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=475)). Tim Keenan applies it to Below the Crown. His first instinct, from Duskers, was to let the player switch chess-piece type mid-run; instead the king, rook or queen is locked for the whole run, which narrows each run's possibility space ("building some walls") while common power-ups remain. In RPG terms, letting a player combine a wizard's staff with a warrior's shield maximises within-run variety, while restricting them to one class makes runs more distinct from each other ([Tim Keenan 2026, 8:36:21](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30981)).

### Lessons from Magic drafting

Gavin Verhey's experience designing Magic: The Gathering draft formats converges with Szanton's. Magic signposts archetypes with two-colour gold uncommons, which both suggest a strategy and tell a half-committed drafter that a colour pair is open upstream, so new players can "hop on rails" for their first drafts ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 5:50](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=350)). Bloomburrow went further and gave every colour pair an animal type, so seeing an otter or a lizard tells you the colours and the mechanical through-line; Wizards' data shows creature-type decks are hugely popular handholds ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 36:27](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=2187)). But signposts that are too strong make the format shallow: the best play becomes taking a gold card early and forcing those colours with no further decisions ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 6:45](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=405)). Bloomburrow onboarded easily but felt shallow to players drafting 30 or 40 times; its fast synergistic decks crowded out offbeat strategies and it had fewer sideways build-arounds than other sets. Verhey describes this as a deliberate pendulum swing from set to set ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 38:00](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=2280)).

His techniques for keeping the thirtieth draft fresh, which he suggests are probably the same ones roguelike designers use ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 7:02](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=422)):

- Strange build-around uncommons that only show up now and then and create a "build my weird deck around it" moment.
- Enough mana fixing to allow splashes and an "eleventh option" like five-colour decks.
- Many interactions among simple commons for players to keep discovering.
- Modal cards that fold situational answers into main-deckable ones (a creature with a hate effect, or "draw two or bounce a green creature"), so the worst case is still useful ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 23:59](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=1439)).
- Balancing format speed as well as colours: if only aggressive cards are good the format is fast, if only control cards are good it is slow. A "+2 power to all creatures" instant at common guarantees an aggressive option even in a slow format ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 30:09](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=1809)).

### Variety at scale

Casey Yano designs Slay the Spire content by starting from a goal strategy and funnelling players toward it so they get an "aha" moment, and cuts anything that doesn't interact interestingly with other content, however strong; a low-HP berserker archetype didn't really work for the game. He cites a rare combo of a relic letting you play status cards and a card dealing damage after five cards played, and says the team makes sure such rare cases can happen ([Casey Yano 2022, 23:26](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=1406)).

How large should the space be? Ben McGraw's Dungeons of Dredmor, whose creation screen came up earlier, lets players pick 7 of 55 flat-cost skills, 55-choose-7 builds, a space Johnny-type combo seekers love but too large to plan or balance ([Ben McGraw 2017, 19:13](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1153)). He concludes that offering many rule-changing choices up front attracts those players at the price of more possibility than anyone can handle before release, so you either keep tweaking or accept it ([Ben McGraw 2017, 24:24](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1464)). Shawn Main frames the same quantity as a goal: ask how many unique combinations your choices provide; Lab of Legends' 50-60 items across 500-600 cards produce combinations even he had never seen ([Shawn Main 2021, 14:33](https://youtu.be/WLBJJTc6LWI?t=873)).

bhauth's analysis of DCSS adds a quantitative lever: the cost curve. If the cost of skills or items is linear with power, players pour everything into one or two things, which bhauth says happens in Brogue and partly explains its few viable strategies, a counterpoint to the build variety credited to Brogue earlier in this chapter; exponential costs push an even spread; polynomial costs, as in DCSS's skill system, give a good mix and more viable builds ([bhauth 2020, 14:48](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=888)). DCSS's replayability comes from species, background and god combinations, hundreds of items and spells (hundreds of viable caster strategies built around about three spell schools), and resistances found during a run changing which enemies are threatening ([bhauth 2020, 14:21](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=861)). Asura forces variety differently, generating a fresh skill tree each game that offers only 16 of about 80 skills across four branches ([Dustin Freeman 2020, 6:46](https://youtu.be/8HDmpu7Kp-A?t=406)).

**In practice:** keep clusters weak and well connected through overlapping categories, bound what each reward source can do so offers are readable, check that your challenge curve does not make most synergies irrelevant, and cap how much one run can collect so builds stay distinct.

## Broken on purpose: power fantasy, exploits and balance

Most genres treat a dominant strategy as a bug. Several talks argue that roguelikes are different: a rare build that breaks the game is part of the promise.

### The permission to break the game

The Against the Storm team identified the ultimate power fantasy as the most important element they found: you play to find the one magical build that turns up one time in twenty and absolutely breaks the game. In other genres that would collapse play to one strategy; in roguelikes it is the point ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 5:32](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=332)). Ben McGraw agrees that broken things can be fun: Dredmor's most active community period centred on discovering exploits, with the team patching in response; he grants that some destructive interactions warrant nerfs but urges letting players have fun ([Ben McGraw 2017, 21:29](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1289)). He names the pattern the "Disgaea effect": balanced at low levels, broken by design at high ones. Disgaea's story is beatable around level 60 while extra content runs to level 9999; single-player games can get away with it because brokenness doesn't ruin another player's day, and in Master of Magic the busted late interactions are what keep it fun for him ([Ben McGraw 2017, 23:06](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1386)).

Courtney Liessen describes what the player should feel: that they are "cheating" by combining systems as intended to get benefits they believe the developer never intended. She separates this from literal cheating (save editing, exploits), from simply overpowering enemies and from cheesing a system out of existence, such as finding a spot pathfinding cannot reach; the real thing feels like a secret you get away with, and makes players feel smart ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 2:54](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=174)). Her Monster Train run is the example: growing a minion three times boosts its stats but uses more floor capacity, an apparently fixed trade-off, until an upgrade shrank a giant to minimum size without reducing its stats and clone upgrades duplicated it repeatedly. Years later she still remembers the run ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 8:32](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=512)).

> Giving players a way to ignore what appeared to be important balancing points in a game is a fantastic way to make them feel they are cheating. — [Courtney Liessen 2024, 8:32](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=512)

Reality Break builds the feeling into its core mechanic. A lightning bolt marks any element the player can rewrite, escalating from item stats to equipment-class requirements, mission time limits, hazards, cooldowns, level caps and treasure crates; a warship-sized item can be rewritten to fighter class and visibly shrinks in the inventory, against the trope that you need a bigger ship first ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 9:35](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=575)). Dylan Gedig adds the audience's view: leave room for builds to combine in crazy ways, including ones that backfire, because streamers whose builds hurt themselves, who laugh that they flew too close to the sun and retry, produce what gets shared most ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 26:28](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1588)).

### Balance by situation, not by number

If power is welcome, how do you keep it in check? Brian Walker's answer for Brogue is to make abilities as powerful as possible and balance them by situationality instead of dialling them down. Creatures entangled in spiderwebs are hit 100% of the time (an earlier version used a -4 modifier); lava instantly kills any creature that neither flies nor is immune to fire, but you have to find it and lure monsters there. Strong situational effects invite optimal players to exploit them and make each character feel different from the last, so the game tells different stories ([Brian Walker 2016, 13:39](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=819)).

Dan DiIorio reaches a compatible rule from Luck be a Landlord: boring content goes unused whatever its power level. His card-suit symbols first boosted all adjacent suits and were overpowered, then only same-colour suits and were boring; adding a small secondary effect, an extra coin if you have at least three suits, got players using them, which beat nudging values or appearance rates ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 4:15](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=255)). His job, he says, is to make content exciting, not powerful: armour with +12 defence that breaks after two hits is more exciting than a plain +5, even if weaker, and could combo with gear that pays out when armour breaks. He added effects to many symbols that had none, and those effects create interactions he never planned ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 8:58](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=538)). Walker and DiIorio converge: the lever is what an effect does and when, not its number.

### Balance still matters

Against the permission stands the experience of Andrew Aversa with Tangledeep. Balance matters even in single player, because a far-too-strong or far-too-weak class produces drastically different experiences: one Steam review called the game impossibly hard and broken, another came from a player who beat it first try, and both were negative. His response was to show a difficulty rank next to each job, lock very hard jobs (like the Gambler, whose escape goes in a random direction) behind a short unlock, and remove things that were absurdly strong or weak ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 21:32](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1292)). Gavin Verhey explains why roguelikes can tolerate more than Magic can: in a PvE game many players will happily pick a harder class for the challenge, and a weak wizard can be buffed in a patch, while in PvP people gravitate to the strongest strategy and Magic must wait for the next set ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 32:44](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=1964)). And McGraw, for all his enthusiasm, warns that balancing massive combinatorics is a long slog of nerfs, tweaks, bans and counter-skills; even a mathematical exchange rate between skills will miss interactions ([Ben McGraw 2017, 20:29](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1229)).
