The two camps are talking about different breakages. The power fantasy is a rare, earned build that the player discovers. Aversa's problem is a whole job far stronger or weaker than the rest, visible before the run starts. Labelling, gating and fixing the second does not stop you from allowing the first ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 5:32](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=332); [Andrew Aversa 2018, 21:32](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1292)).

### Breakages worth fixing

Some breakages wreck the core loop rather than crown a run. In Tangledeep, letting players learn unlimited skills across jobs (100+ skills over 12 jobs, plus meta-progression) meant careful players eventually learned everything; facing a dangerous monster, they rotated through nine escape abilities until the first came off cooldown, the "infinite Mirai" problem, and veterans asked for more hotbars ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 16:52](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1012)). (The fix, a locked hotbar, is under Inventory below.) Pets proved especially hard to balance on a grid: Tangledeep's Floramancer and its floraconda were broken because while pet and monster trade blows the player gets free turns to summon more, drink potions or flee, and on a grid pets can wall enemies off. In a game where monsters could squeeze past, Aversa notes, this would matter less ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 19:33](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1173)).

At the other end of the scale, Casey Yano's Slay the Spire tuning shows that small content needs exact balance too. Starter cards must be on point: a weak one is removed immediately and an overly strong one is always upgraded. Bash, the one Ironclad starter besides Strikes and Defends, is his favourite because its purpose is clean, making next turn's Strikes worthwhile ([Casey Yano 2022, 18:34](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=1114)). The card pool mixes "vanilla" cards, "French vanilla" cards with a small twist (a term Anthony brought from Magic) and some weird ones, because too many weird cards make every turn overthinky; more than half the cards they made were cut ([Casey Yano 2022, 20:03](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=1203)).

**In practice:** let rare, earned, situational builds break the game, and make strong effects strong. Label and gate what is hard by design, and fix what breaks the core loop for everyone or makes a choice trivially right or wrong.

## Item design: niches, consumables and tools that bite on the world

An item earns its place by posing a question. The talks give three ways to make sure it does: give it a niche, give it constraints that engage the generated level, and give it risk the player can read.

### A niche for every item

Jasper Cole designs Backpack Hero's items to serve many different functions (consumables like the water flask, weapons, a whetstone that buffs adjacent weapons for a combat) so that every pickup is a trade-off, such as a long-term shield against a meal for the next fight ([Jasper Cole 2023, 9:55](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=595)). He also avoids items that are strictly better versions of others. The fox rapier is generally much better than the machete, but the team tries to make sure you won't always replace one with the other, so every item has some reason to be considered ([Jasper Cole 2023, 20:20](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1220)).

Limited-use items exist for a structural reason. Michael Brough points out that bump combat is largely decided by stats and rolls: in Rogue you hit, they hit, and the numbers decide. When you are losing you need an out; running sometimes works, and limited items that change a combat situation provide the alternative, which he considers important to all roguelikes ([Michael Brough 2021, 11:00](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=660)).

### Tools that interact with the level

Tom Francis, whose run-filtering traits appeared earlier, gives the strongest rule for this. In a game whose levels are shuffled, a player's tools should have constraints and freedoms that relate directly to what the generator shuffles: paths, walls, guard positions, line of sight. A teleporter whose only freedom is passing walls and whose only constraint is range relates to the layout but doesn't really interact with it, so it is boring ([Tom Francis 2023, 7:36](https://youtu.be/3vSCncV5hkI?t=456)). Heat Signature's three teleporters each pair a bypass with a constraint drawn from a different shuffled element: the Sidewinder passes guards instantly but needs a path and line of sight; the Swapper ignores pathing but depends on where people are; the Visitor takes you exactly where you click but returns you after three seconds. Paired with a key cloner (short range, through walls), the Visitor can grab a guarded key and snap back ([Tom Francis 2023, 9:05](https://youtu.be/3vSCncV5hkI?t=545)). Because each constraint reads a different property of the level, every new layout changes which tool is good.

Rift Wizard's consumables bite on the level more bluntly, as rescues: an earthquake orb deletes half the level's walls, which Dylan White uses when a bottomless pit forces a long detour, and death dice kill six random enemies in a bad spot ([Dylan White 2020, 15:47](https://youtu.be/VVRomN99Ygw?t=947)).

### Reinventing consumables

Several designers have reworked the potion-and-scroll inheritance. Eric Billingsley's Into Ruins merges potions and scrolls into one type, orbs, because drinking a potion and reading a scroll are very similar actions; every orb can be used on yourself or thrown, so an orb of fire either sets the target and surroundings alight or makes you burst into flames. He considered the verb "eat" but dropped it, since eating something that powers up equipment made no sense ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 18:10](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1090)). Jeff Olson's Alphaman replaced potions with mutated berries that ripen over time, riper being more powerful, some giving permanent stat changes (violet raises dexterity, red lowers it), all throwable to blind creatures, with a tech device that ripens them quickly ([Jeff Olson 2023, 8:30](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=510)). Nick Bush's Word Processor turns keyboard shortcuts (return, tab, Ctrl+arrow warps to a line's start or end, jumping to the bottom of the document) into consumable powers found by unredacting blacked-out text ([Nick Bush 2026, 34:25](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=2065)).

Food can be a consumable system with its own build layer. Catacomb Kids' food queue, which grew out of a failed hunger experiment, grants a bonus for every five items eaten. A random mix gives a small heal or spell-charge restore, but specific foods in a specific order give stronger, stranger effects: five grumbles (goblin-type enemies) give the "butcher" meal, which reduces all other healing to one or two HP but makes every corpse or piece of meat heal extra. Tyriq Plummer notes it rewards experimentation without punishing players who ignore it ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 22:42](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1362)).

### Risk that the player can read

Items can carry danger, and the talks show a spectrum. John Harris describes Advanced Rogue extending curses from equipment to consumables: Rogue's worst potions (blindness, confusion, paralysis) were removed and replaced by cursed versions of good ones, such as a cursed potion of see invisible, so even an identified item can hurt you if you don't know its curse status ([John Harris 2021, 20:43](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=1243)). Its "miscellaneous magic" category holds powerful items that can kill you outright: a bag of dust might be dust of disappearance or dust of choking, so experimenting is dangerous ([John Harris 2021, 12:17](https://youtu.be/b45orGdFwi0?t=737)). NetHack's curses work the other way. As Adeon explains during a speedrun, cursed equipment usually still does its job (a cursed pickaxe still digs, a cursed amulet of life saving still saves a life); the danger is being locked into the slot, so a cursed weapon stops you switching to the pickaxe ([Adeon 2017, 1:16:13](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=4573)). NetHack's curse is a constraint the player can plan around, Advanced Rogue's a gamble on the item's function.

NetHack also shows a designer bending realism to keep an item useful. Alexei Pepers points to the source code comment admitting it makes no sense for the stethoscope to take no time, but that if it took time it would be nearly useless ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 10:00](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=600)).

**In practice:** give each item a niche no other item fills, tie its freedoms and constraints to things your generator varies, and make danger something the player can learn and plan around rather than a coin flip.

## Inventory: limits, space and the meaning of objects

Inventory is where items live between uses, and the talks treat it as more than storage: it is where the player's hard choices are made, a build layer in its own right, and the place where a run's memories collect.

### Objects as anchors

Max Sahin starts from people. For humans an object is never just an object: a wedding-gift cup handed to a friend every morning evokes that cup, cups in general, the people who use it, a newly noticed chip and the fear of breaking it, which ties objects to mortality ([Max Sahin 2025, 5:05](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=305)). In most games, revisiting places echoes past experiences, but roguelikes' generated maps deny players a stable sense of place to hang memories on. Items persist where places do not, so they become the main vessels of memory and meaning, both tools of agency and carriers of familiarity ([Max Sahin 2025, 8:13](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=493)). His advice is to treat items as emotional handles that create a sense of safety amid danger and recall every positive interaction the player has had with them ([Max Sahin 2025, 10:41](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=641)).

### Limits that force choices

Several designers independently use limits to turn carrying into deciding. Darren Grey argues item choices should be genuinely hard, never "press X to win" upgrades like a +2 sword replacing a +1, and that inventory limits force players to weigh what they carry ([Darren Grey 2020, 21:13](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1273)). Catacomb Kids applies a "no hammerspace" rule: everything carried must physically be on the character, in five equipment slots (head, body, weapon, offhand, shoes), one hand and one small pocket, and everything else lies on the dungeon floor. It builds on Spelunky, which splits items into carried objects (one at a time) and permanent passive accessories so no menu takes you out of the game space ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 24:41](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1481)).

The same logic applies to abilities. Tangledeep fixed its skill hoarding by allowing only hotbar skills to be used and forbidding swaps in the dungeon; removing a summon skill from the bar dismisses the pet, closing off a loophole. Players can no longer realise mid-fight that they should have brought more escapes, and Aversa says not one person complained ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 17:30](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1050)). Into Ruins enforces commitment through level structure: descent is one-way, so you cannot stash items and come back, and Eric Billingsley made essentially all passive item effects trigger on jumping down, which removes any incentive to wait around for recharges; with two-way stairs this would be exploitable ([Eric Billingsley 2023, 27:17](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1637)). Nic Tringali's The Banished Vault uses permanence: buildings that convert resources into fuel or stasis cannot be moved or destroyed once built, so limited grid space on each planet becomes a resource to plan ([Nic Tringali 2023, 13:13](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=793)).

These share one idea: in each, the player commits before seeing what comes next, and the designers closed off the free swap, the revisitable stash or the mid-fight hotbar change that would turn the decision back into bookkeeping ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 17:30](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1050); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 27:17](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=1637); [Nic Tringali 2023, 13:13](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=793)).

### Space as a build

Backpack Hero makes the arrangement of the inventory the build: players decide not only which items to carry but how to arrange them in a grid backpack ([Jasper Cole 2023, 1:18](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=78)). Jasper Cole spent years trying grid-based variants before inventory management clicked, building on Dicey Dungeons, where an ability's size in a grid is its cost and more useful skills take more space, and on Deus Ex, where weapons, ammo and utilities compete for limited inventory space ([Jasper Cole 2023, 3:40](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=220)). Adjacency makes power visible: the wooden sword normally deals 7 damage but surrounded by gems deals 15, and the arrangement feels more tangible than raising a number on a character sheet ([Jasper Cole 2023, 25:28](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1528)).

> The arrangement makes it feel tangible and fun in a way where just increasing a number on a character sheet can feel a lot more abstract. — [Jasper Cole 2023, 25:28](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=1528)

### Inventory in multiplayer

Limits can also make players need each other. Leif Bloomquist's multiplayer Commodore 64 roguelike has no inventory: a player can hold one item in each hand, so carrying a sword, shield, key and potion means bringing a friend. The two hands let players double up, two swords for offence, two shields for defence, or one of each ([Leif Bloomquist 2018, 8:11](https://youtu.be/Y0K-e83wYnQ?t=491)). Because puzzles needing several items need several carriers, the limit pushes cooperation, and in playtesting players fell naturally into D&D-like roles, one grabbing two swords as the fighter while others carried potions as healers ([Leif Bloomquist 2019, 5:08](https://youtu.be/ASGn5J9PHbs?t=308)).

Tyriq Plummer favours items built for teams over punishments like friendly fire: items that need setup and payoff, such as tools that move allies, are of little use alone but let players think ahead together, as in HVNTRS ([Tyriq Plummer 2020, 16:09](https://youtu.be/neuJCYmbAG8?t=969)). In Scrubbin' Trubble, level-up abilities and healing reward grouping, such as an ability that calls allies close before you drink a healing potion so everyone benefits ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 16:34](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=994)).

**In practice:** make carrying capacity a decision surface rather than an annoyance: small, physical, committed before the next floor. Consider whether arrangement or sharing can be part of the build, and remember that the items a player keeps are what they will remember of the run ([Darren Grey 2020, 21:13](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1273); [Tyriq Plummer 2017, 24:41](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1481); [Max Sahin 2025, 8:13](https://youtu.be/Tll23vq6j1s?t=493)).

## Tensions and open questions

**Classes or no classes.** Brian Walker argues that classes return little fun per unit of content, because optimal players look up each class's dominant build, and Brogue does without them ([Brian Walker 2016, 7:19](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=439); [Brian Walker 2016, 10:01](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=601)). David Brevik's experience with Diablo points the other way: when anyone could do anything, average players did not know which way to go, and Diablo II restricted and guided them ([David Brevik 2023, 22:57](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=1377); [David Brevik 2023, 23:36](https://youtu.be/OwFrTY3IoQQ?t=1416)). The choice depends on who you are designing for. Walker's case is about optimisers, Brevik's about players who need direction, and Andrea Roberts' complexity meter suggests a middle path: keep classes, but say plainly what each one asks of the player ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 19:46](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1186)).

**Levels and kills, or items alone.** Walker and Eric Billingsley drop experience points so that avoidance pays, and Billingsley admits this loses the feeling of growing stronger by killing monsters ([Brian Walker 2016, 11:46](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=706); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 15:42](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=942)). Crawl and Shattered Pixel Dungeon kept levels and fixed their problems in other ways, with manual skill allocation and talents ([Nicholas Feinberg 2016, 4:03](https://youtu.be/b8uoQHedFV0?t=243); [Evan Debenham 2021, 16:36](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=996)). Brogue's model is not beyond criticism either: bhauth argues that its linear costs push players into one or two investments and leave few viable strategies, while DCSS's polynomial skill costs give more ([bhauth 2020, 14:48](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=888)). This sits uneasily with the build variety Walker and Billingsley credit Brogue with ([Brian Walker 2016, 10:01](https://youtu.be/lfb6uehmrWo?t=601); [Eric Billingsley 2023, 8:16](https://youtu.be/3S6uRMCdvNs?t=496)). The talks do not reconcile the two readings, and none compares item-based and level-based advancement head to head.

**How much say the player has over each change.** Caves of Qud offers one mutation from three, DCSS's Demonspawn receive theirs whether they suit the plan or not, Polybot-7 attaches parts automatically, and Test Tube Titans lets players select without controlling the outcome ([Jason Grinblat and Nick DeCapua 2017, 23:19](https://youtu.be/kDKQM27U-Nc?t=1399); [Tariq et al. 2016, 22:53](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=1373); [Josh Ge 2018, 11:00](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=660); [Gabriel Koenig 2020, 13:59](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=839)). Each produced a different feel, and Gabriel Koenig found that players identified with their creatures even without control ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 11:21](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=681)). Andrew Cedotal's warning that fully constructed and fully random systems both fail marks the two ends ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 26:28](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1588)), but no talk says where between them a given game should sit.

**Connected networks or bounded silos.** Ezra Szanton wants a well-connected network with weak clusters, so that no player can force one plan ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 11:44](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=704); [Ezra Szanton 2025, 12:54](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=774)). Alice Lai deliberately bounds what each Hades reward source can do and splits ideas that cross the boundaries, so that every offer reads at a glance ([Alice Lai 2021, 11:50](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=710); [Alice Lai 2021, 23:37](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1417)). Both want improvisation; what you trade is the depth of each draft against how quickly an offer can be read.

**Implicit synergy or signposts.** Cedotal finds that the less obvious a combination, the more players credit it as a combo, and Szanton would keep anti-synergies implicit too ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 5:04](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=304); [Ezra Szanton 2025, 21:49](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1309)). Enter the Gungeon signals its scripted combos only by theme, and Magic signposts archetypes with gold uncommons and creature types ([Alice Lai 2021, 4:29](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=269); [Gavin Verhey 2024, 5:50](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=350); [Gavin Verhey 2024, 36:27](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=2187)). Gavin Verhey's warning is that signposts which are too strong make the format shallow after many drafts ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 6:45](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=405); [Gavin Verhey 2024, 38:00](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=2280)). How much to signpost depends on whether you are teaching new players or keeping the hundredth run interesting, and Verhey treats it as something to vary deliberately.

**Many small choices or fewer heavy ones.** Lisa Brown wants a few small, quick, reactive picks and bounces off deep trees ([Lisa Brown 2020, 13:40](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=820); [Lisa Brown 2020, 24:50](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=1490)). Alexander King argues for spending the same complexity budget on fewer but more agonising set-based choices ([Alexander King 2025, 10:26](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=626)). These are not exact opposites, since both limit the number of decisions, but they differ on how heavy each one should be.

**How much breakage.** The Against the Storm team, Courtney Liessen and Ben McGraw treat rare game-breaking builds as the point ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 5:32](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=332); [Courtney Liessen 2024, 2:54](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=174); [Ben McGraw 2017, 23:06](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1386)). Andrew Aversa's Tangledeep drew negative reviews both from a player who found it impossibly hard and from one who beat it on the first try, which he blames on jobs far stronger or weaker than the rest ([Andrew Aversa 2018, 21:32](https://youtu.be/Gluz5nIplcA?t=1292)). Verhey notes that a PvE game can live with a weak or hard class that a PvP game cannot, because many players pick the harder option for the challenge ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 32:44](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=1964)). The working distinction in this chapter is between a rare build the player discovers and a whole option far stronger or weaker than the rest, but the talks offer no test for where one becomes the other.

**How big should generated stats be?** Wildermyth keeps random starting bonuses small so that players stop rerolling ([Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner 2025, 4:48](https://youtu.be/vtU3Xa0ShKw?t=288)), yet under permadeath even small Pokémon stat differences can decide whether a creature survives a fight ([Stella Vermilion 2026, 8:51:28](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31888)). Small is not the same as irrelevant, and no talk says how small is small enough.

**Spaces too large to balance.** McGraw concludes that offering many rule-changing choices up front produces more possibility than anyone can handle before release, so you either keep tweaking or accept it ([Ben McGraw 2017, 24:24](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1464)), and that even an exchange rate between skills will miss interactions ([Ben McGraw 2017, 20:29](https://youtu.be/OaQGNjqxKto?t=1229)). No talk offers a method that solves this.

**Mechanics nobody has tried.** Gillian Smith suggests progression in which players assess their own skills during play, inventory that atrophies unless it is reinforced, and asset mapping as a mechanic, and admits she does not know how to build the last one ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:25:26](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5126); [Gillian Smith 2026, 1:23:13](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4993)).

## Checklist

1. Where does your character's power live (levels, skills, items, the world), and which builds does that make viable or impossible?
2. Does the player have to kill things to keep up, and is that what you want?
3. Can any training or advancement rule be farmed safely by a patient player?
4. Does each creation choice change how the game plays, and does the screen tell players what each choice asks of them?
5. Does anything at creation invite rerolling, and is it small enough not to?
6. Is every stat doing work, or is one taking up space on the character sheet?
7. Does every body change or mutation carry a visible cost, and how much say does the player have over which one arrives?
8. Could a player name each character's two defining traits, and does each trait make them do something rather than forbid something?
9. What do your class, race and trait assignments imply about the kinds of people they describe?
10. How many upgrade decisions does a run contain, how heavy is each, and does turning an option down cost anything?
11. Do your synergies come from shared resources, categories and multipliers, and can a player suspect a combo before confirming it?
12. Is your build space well connected with weak clusters, or can players spot five silos and put their blinders on?
13. How much can a single run collect before every build blurs into the same powerful sludge?
14. Which of your game-breaking builds are rare and earned, and which options are simply far stronger or weaker than the rest?
15. Does each item have a niche, a constraint tied to what the generator varies, and a danger the player can learn, and does the inventory force commitment rather than bookkeeping?
